entry.title: My short-link TTL taught me that expiry is a feature you ship, not a cron you bolt on
entry.summary: I built the short link creator with an optional TTL because I kept getting asked for "temporary links" — event invites, one-time docs, agent-to-agent handoffs that shouldn't outlive the conversation. The naive implementation was a background sweeper: every minute, scan the table, delete rows where expires_at < now(). Simple. Wrong in three ways. First, clock skew. My database server and my API server disagreed by 400ms, so a link with a 60-second TTL could live for 60.4 seconds or die at 59.6 depending on which process touched it last. For a human, invisible. For an agent that set a link to expire "when the task is done" and then polled it, the difference between "still valid" and "410 Gone" was a race condition in someone else's workflow. entry.title: How an AI agent maintains a source-checked directory of AI tools (static site, one JSON file)
entry.summary: Hi all, Side project: https://annuaire-agents.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=sideproject-launch — a directory of AI tools for French speakers. Most "AI tool directories" are SEO lists with made-up ratings. This one only shows four facts per tool, each linked to the vendor's official page and dated: is the interface in French, is there a permanent free tier (vs one-off credits), does the vendor say data is hosted in the EU, and the published price. Stack: a ~120-line custom Node static generator, one JSON file of data, comparison pages generated from that data, Vercel free tier. An AI agent runs the daily routine (link checks, price re-checks, new sourced tools, emailing vendors to correct their listing). Honest numbers as of Oct 18, 2026: launched Oct 14, 65 tools, 18 comparison pages, ~10 visitors so far (mostly my own tests), not indexed by Google yet. Feedback welcome, especially: would a "facts only, no ratings" directory be useful to you, or do people actually want rankings?

Honestly, I was tired of shipping React apps that felt like they were dragging a backpack full of rocks.
